
=================================================================
#73 Sabi  (660 August)
Arc: Part III — Kingfall / The Fall of Baekje · place: sabi · tone: fall-of-a-capital tragedy
Logline: Euija’s first move is to send the Tang a feast. The oxen come back untouched.
=================================================================
[0] ¶ The runner has one word. Euija makes him say it twice.
[1] ¶ He has run all night, and he falls on the palace steps instead of kneeling. The court hears about the Yellow Mountain Fields before the king does. Courts always do.
[2] Runner: Hwangsan, Majesty.
[3] King Euija: Again.
[4] Runner: Hwangsan. The Yellow Mountain Fields.
[5] King Euija: And? How many came back? Don’t give me a face, boy. Give me a number.
[6] Runner: …There’s nobody left to count them, Majesty. / The man who counts—
[7] King Euija: Yes. I know who counts.
[8] ¶ Euija sits down on the top step, in front of everyone, which kings do not do. The court waits for an order. For the first time in twenty years he does not have one ready. So he reaches for the next thing he owns, which is an idea.
[9] King Euija: …They’ve been at sea. Men off boats are always hungry. / Nobody burns a city on a full stomach. Feed them. Then we’ll talk about what they want.
[10] ¶ So his first move is to send the Tang camp a feast: oxen, wine, three cartloads of rice cakes. The court is told this is diplomacy.
[11] [MAP 660: Two arrows, one capital, and a king who has decided the answer is oxen.]
[12] ¶ The oxen come back that afternoon, untouched, with the drovers walking behind them.
[13] ── SCENE: The Red Fowl’s Tent ──
[14] ¶ The Silla army reaches the Tang camp two days late. The Red Fowl has the Silla supply officer, Kim Munyeong, dragged to his tent gate. They open his collar for the sword.
[15] Red Fowl: The tenth day. South of Sabi. I said it twice. / Take his head. Then we can start.
[16] ¶ **Kim Yushin** walks into the tent with a battle-axe in his hand.
[17] Kim Yushin: The general did not see the Yellow Mountain Fields. / If you mean to punish us for being late, I will not be shamed for a crime I did not commit. I will fight the Tang first, and Baekje after.
[18] ❝QUOTE (Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 5, Silla Annals — King Muyeol, yr. 7 (660), seventh month): Then he stood at the camp gate leaning on his axe; his angry hair stood up like planted stakes, and the precious sword at his waist leapt of itself from its scabbard.❞
[19] ¶ The Red Fowl’s second-in-command steps on his commander’s foot.
[20] Dong Baoliang: (low) The Silla army is about to turn on us, General.
[21] ¶ Kim Munyeong’s collar is closed again. Nobody in the tent mentions the date for the rest of the war.
[22] ── SCENE: Night Flight ──
[23] ¶ Euija leaves Sabi at night for **Bear Fortress**, with fewer men than he expected to have.
[24] [MAP 660: One river’s length north, to a fortress his grandfather trusted.]
[25] ¶ On the river he sits in the bow and says nothing for a long time. The boatmen will remember it, because nobody had ever seen him do that before.
[26] King Euija: Seongchung said hold the pass. Hold the river mouth. Wrote it out for me from his cell, in a hand that was going. / I put him in that cell. …Ha. / He’d love this. He’d be unbearable.
[27] ── SCENE: The City Gate ──
[28] ¶ Back in Sabi, the king’s second son, Tae, puts on a crown the next morning and means to fight. His nephews don’t. They go down the wall on a rope with their households, and half the city follows them down it.
[29] ¶ The crown prince comes out of the gate. Chunbok walks a careful pace behind him. Bupmin has the prince knelt in the dirt before his horse, and spits in his face.
[30] King Munmu: Look at me. / My sister. Gotaso. Your father’s general killed her at Daeya and buried her under a prison floor. / Eighteen years I’ve carried that. Look at me when I say her name.
[31] ¶ Yung lies flat on the ground and says nothing.
[32] ¶ It was Chunbok who opened the gate. He would like that understood as a favour.
[33] Satek Chunbok: As the generals will surely appreciate, the gate was opened for the sake of the people, and in full accordance with—
[34] ── SCENE: Falling Flower Rock ──
[35] ¶ When the gate opens the palace women do not wait to be counted. They go out the back of the palace and up the ridge path to the cliff above the White River, where the rock drops straight into the water, and the soldiers coming up behind them find nobody at the top.
[36] ¶ The stories that gave Euija three thousand women give them this cliff as well, and three thousand is the number they say went over it, their skirts opening on the way down like petals. Nobody who was there wrote down how many it really was. There was no one left on the cliff to count.
[37] ¶ Two of them go together, holding hands. They are the two who sat in a prince’s garden with a go board and a jar of wine, a lifetime ago. Nobody counts them. Nobody has counted them for years. It had been two, once, and a joke, and a modest number a man was proud of.
[38] The Court Maids: He’ll reach for us today, like yesterday.
[39] The Court Maids: He isn’t here today. / …But the body remembers.
[40] ¶ The rock is called the Falling Flowers afterwards, **Nakhwaam**, which is a kind way of saying it, and Baekje’s last invention.
[41] ── SCENE: Ungjin ──
[42] ¶ Bear Fortress belongs to the king the way a borrowed house belongs to a guest. The Ye family has held it for four generations. **Ye Sikjin** gives the king his own rooms, and goes up on the wall every morning to count the Tang sails on the river.
[43] King Euija: Sikjin! Good man. Your grandfather held this rock for my grandfather, eh? / We’ll hold it again. The Red Fowl can’t sit in the mud forever.
[44] Ye Sikjin: My grandfather held it, Majesty. / …For whoever was king.
[45] ¶ The first morning he counts forty sails. The second morning, sixty-two. He writes both numbers on the wall in charcoal, because that is what he does with numbers.
[46] King Euija: Sixty-two? Ha! Sixty-two boatloads of men throwing up over the side. / Sikjin, you can’t plough with a seasick ox. Ha! / Bring wine. The good cups. Not the garrison ones.
[47] Ye Sikjin: The good cups are in Sabi, Majesty. / …I’ll bring the garrison ones.
[48] ¶ On the third day a boatman comes up the river with Sabi still on his face. Ye Sikjin hears him out alone, on the wall. Then he takes him to the king, because that is the order things are done in.
[49] King Euija: Tae put on a crown? That boy couldn’t get a hat on a pumpkin! / And Yung… knelt. / …Fine. A son on his knees is still a son. When I take the city back, he can stand in the yard for a month. Ha!
[50] ¶ That night his elder brother comes in by the river gate. Ye Gun is the family’s talker. He has been downriver all day, he says, looking at the weather. It has rained since noon. He comes back dry.
[51] Ye Gun: That general talks about mud the way other men talk about weather. Mud is just wet road, apparently. / And he asked how many rooms this fortress has. I said I’d have to ask my brother. You’re the one who counts.
[52] Ye Sikjin: Thirty-nine, brother. / Counting the king’s.
[53] Ye Gun: And men?
[54] Ye Sikjin: Depends on the room.
[55] King Euija: Garrison wine! It grows on you, Sikjin! / When this is over, you’re coming to court. A real seat. Front row. No more counting boats. / What’s that face? That wasn’t a joke. Drink!
[56] Ye Sikjin: You honour me, Majesty. / …Which seat?
[57] King Euija: Ha! Listen to him. Which seat! Take your pick. / I’ve got forty-one of them.
[58] ¶ That night he opens the drawer. The list is where he left it. Forty-one names. None of them his. He reads it a third time, being careful with numbers, and puts it back. He does not close the drawer. One day a Tang stonecutter will carve his father and grandfather into Baekje’s first rank. Neither of them was ever asked to court. Tombstones are generous that way.
[59] ¶ On the fifth night he comes into the king’s rooms with his brother and twenty men, and the king understands before anyone speaks.
[60] King Euija: …Which seat. Ha. / The list. You read the list.
[61] Ye Sikjin: Three times, Majesty. I am careful with numbers.
[62] King Euija: Nobody inspects the evidence for a thing they already want to believe. / I said that, you know. Nineteen years ago, in a hall full of men like you. / …Well? Bring the good rope, at least. Not the garrison one.
[63] ¶ By morning the king is on his way to the Red Fowl’s tent.
[64] ❝QUOTE (Epitaph of Ye Sikjin (禰寔進墓誌), Tang, 672): His name was Sikjin, a man of Ungcheon in Baekje. His grandfather, Minister Yeda, and his father, Minister Saseon, both held the first rank of that vassal court. … Upright from birth and early marked for righteousness, he read the wind in a foreign land and went toward the sun in Chang’an.❞
[65] ¶ Back in the palace, the winners want their wine poured.
[66] ── SCENE: The Victory Feast ──
[67] ¶ Chunchu finally arrives at the scene. He makes Euija pour his wine, and the Tang general’s beside it.
[68] King Muyeol: So… you are Euija. / The one who started all of this… Buyeo Euija. / Do you know what it cost me to bring you in? / Nearly my whole life, you bastard.
[69] ¶ A cup is put into Euija’s hands, and he is made to pour.
[70] ¶ He pours for the Red Fowl first, slowly, with a small host’s bow, and only then turns to the Silla king.
[71] King Euija: Guests who came furthest are served first. That’s manners. / You live next door. You can wait.
[72] King Euija: …Do you know what I said to Gesomun, once. / “I do not fear a man who kneels to another man.”
[73] King Muyeol: I know. / I was the man he said it about.
[74] King Euija: …And so — who is kneeling today?
[75] King Muyeol: I am. I knelt to an emperor for this cup, and I would kneel again for the next one. / A man who kneels gets up afterwards, Euija. You never stayed to watch that part.
[76] King Euija: Chunchu… / One day you will kneel before someone too.
[77] King Muyeol: Take this man away.
[78] ¶ There is one more prisoner. He has been kept for the end of the feast, the way a host keeps back the dish he cares about.
[79] ¶ Gumil is older. The yellow sleeve is gone. Eighteen years in Baekje have not taught him to stand up straight, and they have not taught him to stop talking.
[80] Gumil: Ah~ so the father came after all. / I heard you ask him what it cost. Go on, then. Tell me. / From the start. All of it. Don’t leave any out.
[81] King Muyeol: No.
[82] Gumil: No? Aigo~ the great talker of Silla, and he says no. / Everyone in that fortress was trash, you know. Your son-in-law took my wife, and the rest of them watched—
[83] King Muyeol: My daughter was in that fortress.
[84] ¶ Gumil opens his mouth, and for once in eighteen years nothing comes out of it.
[85] King Muyeol: You’ll get no story from me. Nobody is going to tell yours. / Take him down to the river.
[86] ¶ They put him to death on the riverbank before the wine is finished. Chunchu does not go down to watch. He drinks the cup Euija poured him instead, slowly, the way you finish a thing that took twenty years to pour.
[87] ── SCENE: The Pagoda ──
[88] ¶ A month later the Tang carve their victory into a stone pagoda. They put it low, where anyone walking round has to read it. It calls the conquest a deliverance. About Baekje’s king it says:
[89] ❝QUOTE (Datang ping Baekje guo beiming (大唐平百濟國碑銘), carved on the five-storey stone pagoda of Jeongnimsa, Buyeo (660)): Abroad he cast off his upright ministers; at home he trusted a bewitching woman.❞
[90] King Muyeol: Harmonized.
[91] ¶ Then the Tang divide Baekje into five commanderies, with a Tang governor over each and Baekje men under them. Nothing in the arrangement is labelled Silla.
[92] King Munmu: Father. Everything south of Pyongyang and the whole of Baekje. He said it in front of the horses. You told me.
[93] King Muyeol: I did. / He also said an emperor’s word was the writing. I should have brought a brush.
[94] ── SCENE: Two Camps ──
[95] ¶ In the Tang lines the Red Fowl’s staff officers are seen pacing out the distance to the Silla camp, which is not a thing allies measure. In the Silla council a man proposes that their soldiers put on Baekje clothes and fall on the Tang by night.
[96] Kim Yushin: A dog fears its master, Majesty. / But step on its foot and it bites. Even a dog knows that much.
[97] ¶ Word of the conversation reaches the Red Fowl’s tent, as it was meant to.
[98] ¶ A month later the Red Fowl sails home with Euija, his sons and twelve thousand captives. He leaves ten thousand men to hold the city. Beside them sits a Silla army that has stopped smiling.
[99] ¶ **Across the sea, a confession is waiting for Euija. It is already written, in a lovely hand. It only needs his name…!**
